name: BYTE-07
title: Prefill: Why Long Context Feels Broken
subtitle: the wait before the first word

scenes.head: two numbers, one of them is invisible
scenes.vo: Okay, so you paste a long document into a local model and nothing happens for twenty seconds. The model is not broken, and your card is not too slow. You are watching a number that almost nobody measures, called prefill, and it decides how the whole thing feels. Token generation is how fast words come out. Prefill is how long you wait before the first one.

scenes.head: rtx 5090 prefill · glimmer
scenes.vo: On a five-oh-ninety, Muse Glimmer processes a four K prompt at four thousand six hundred and twenty-five tokens a second. At sixteen K it is four thousand three hundred and seventy-three. At sixty-four K it is three thousand six hundred and six. At one twenty-eight K, two thousand eight hundred and six. At two hundred fifty-six K, one thousand eight hundred and seventy-four. Long context costs you, but it degrades gracefully.

cues.1: three thousand six hundred and six
cues.3: one thousand eight hundred and seventy-four

scenes.head: same card · qwen 3.8
scenes.vo: The same card running Qwen three point eight starts at three thousand seven hundred and forty-nine at four K. At sixteen K it is eighteen hundred and twenty-five. At sixty-four K it is seven hundred and seventeen. And at one twenty-eight K it is four hundred and sixty-one tokens a second. That is the number that makes a long context chat feel broken.

scenes.head: what that means in seconds
scenes.vo: Turn it into time. A hundred thousand token prompt at forty-six hundred tokens a second is about twenty-two seconds of waiting. The same prompt at four hundred and sixty-one tokens a second is three and a half minutes, before the model writes a single word. That is the whole difference between an assistant and a loading screen.

scenes.head: why prefill collapses
scenes.vo: Prefill is one big matrix multiplication over the whole prompt, so it scales with prompt length and it is memory bandwidth bound. The longer the prompt, the more of the model's attention you have to compute before you can emit the first token. Generation, by contrast, is one token at a time and barely cares how long the prompt was.
items: one pass over the whole prompt

scenes.head: two honest notes
scenes.vo: Two notes. These are single GPU measurements with full offload, so a machine that splits a model across cards will see different prefill behaviour. And a cached prompt is nearly free on the second run, so the wait you feel is usually the first time only.
items: Prompt caching removes most repeat cost

scenes.head: rtx 3090 prefill
scenes.vo: On a three thousand ninety the numbers are lower but the shape is identical. Glimmer prefills a four K prompt at fourteen hundred and seventy-seven tokens a second. Sixty-four K is eleven hundred. One twenty-eight K is eight hundred and fifty-three. Two hundred fifty-six K is five hundred and eighty-four. Even the old card degrades gracefully on the better optimised model.

scenes.head: qwen 3.8 on the same 3090
scenes.vo: Qwen three point eight on the same card starts at thirteen hundred and eight at four K, which is close enough to Glimmer that you would not notice. By sixty-four K it is seven hundred and seventeen, and that is where the two diverge. Same card, same engine, one model holds its prefill and the other halves it.

cues.h: Qwen three point eight on the same card

scenes.head: prompt caching changes everything
scenes.vo: There is one honest escape hatch. If you send the same long document repeatedly, a cached prompt is nearly free on the second pass, because the prefill work is already done. So the twenty seconds you feel is a first-time cost, not a per-message cost. Agents that re-read the same codebase over and over are exactly the case where caching turns an unusable wait into a normal one.

scenes.head: time to first token at 100k
scenes.vo: Put the three machines side by side at a hundred thousand token prompt. Twenty-two seconds on a five-oh-ninety running Glimmer. Fifty-four seconds on a three thousand ninety. Two hundred and seventeen seconds on the same five-oh-ninety running Qwen three point eight. Same document, same question, a wait that ranges from tolerable to abandoned.

scenes.head: how to measure it yourself
scenes.vo: Measurement is easy and almost nobody does it. Send the longest prompt you realistically use, and time from pressing enter to the first character appearing. That single number predicts whether the tool feels fast, better than any tokens per second figure on a leaderboard. Write it down for two machines and the purchase decision makes itself.

scenes.head: generation vs prefill on one axis
scenes.vo: Put generation and prefill on the same axis and the point becomes obvious. On a five-oh-ninety with Glimmer at four K, prefill is four thousand six hundred and twenty-five and generation is eighty-three. Prefill is fifty-five times faster because it processes the whole prompt in one pass. But at one twenty-eight K, prefill has fallen to twenty-eight hundred while generation has only fallen to seventy-five. Prefill degrades faster than generation does.

cues.0: four thousand six hundred and twenty-five

scenes.head: why benchmarks hide it
scenes.vo: Benchmarks hide prefill for a boring reason. Tokens per second is one number and it is easy to publish, while time to first token depends on the prompt you personally paste, so it does not fit in a table. The result is that every comparison you have ever read is about the number you feel second, and almost none of them are about the number you feel first.
items: easy to publish, easy to compare
depends on your prompt, rarely published

scenes.head: what to expect on your own machine
scenes.vo: On a three thousand ninety, expect prefill around fourteen hundred at short prompts, eleven hundred at sixty-four K, and eight hundred and fifty at one twenty-eight K. If you are seeing far below that, you are either spilling out of VRAM or you are not using the offload path you think you are. Those are the two things worth checking before you blame the model.

cues.h: On a three thousand ninety, expect

scenes.head: caching in practice
scenes.vo: In practice, prompt caching is the single highest leverage setting for long context work. If your tool supports it, keep the stable part of the prompt first and the changing part last, because a cache hit requires the prefix to match exactly. Move one word at the top and you pay the full prefill again. That one habit turns a three minute wait into a two second one.
items: and you pay full price again

scenes.head: the bottom line
scenes.vo: The bottom line is that prefill is the half of performance nobody publishes, and it is the half you feel first. Every time you paste a document, you are watching a benchmark run in real time. Learn what your machine does at your prompt length, and the hardware conversation gets a lot shorter, because you will already know the answer before anyone posts a table.
items: Time to first token is what you feel

scenes.head: the one sentence version
scenes.vo: One sentence. Prefill decides how long you stare at the cursor, generation decides how fast the words arrive, and almost every comparison you have ever read only measures the second one. At a hundred thousand tokens the same card can take twenty-two seconds or two hundred and seventeen depending on the model, and that gap is the entire difference between a tool you use and a tool you stop opening.

scenes.head: close
scenes.vo: So when you compare hardware, do not only compare tokens per second. Compare the time to first token at the prompt length you actually paste. That is the number you feel, and it is the number almost nobody publishes.
